I have enough information to answer.

**I would not recommend turning CH-01 off right now.** Here's why:

**1. CH-01 is the lead chiller and is doing real cooling work.**
CH-01 is currently running at 52.6 kW (26% of its 200 kW rating) on feeder MDB-4, and per the chiller manual it is started as the **lead chiller**; CH-02 (the large 250 kW unit) is only staged in when demand exceeds what CH-01 can handle — right now CH-02 is OFF [source: docs/knowledge/equipment/EQ-07_chiller.md#EQ-07 Chiller Manual > Start-up sequence > Sequence]. Turning the lead chiller off would remove the primary chilled-water capacity without any standby unit ready to take the load.

**2. Cooling appears to be meeting current demand.**
The plant's total demand at the end of the dataset was only ~500 kW against a 1250 kW contract (40% of contract, zero intervals over contract) [data: get_demand]. Chiller load is already modest (52.6 kW), and the plant is nowhere near its demand limit, so there is no pressure to shed the chiller to avoid a penalty.

**3. Chillers share cooling with critical loads.**
MDB-4 (HVAC & chilled water) also supports the chilled-water loop that conditions the server room (DC-01 at 20.5 kW, 82% of rating) and other processes [source: docs/knowledge/equipment/EQ-07_chiller.md#EQ-07 Chiller Manual > Units covered]. Shutting the lead chiller risks raising supply-water temperature and destabilizing cooling for equipment that needs it.

**4. The energy saving is small and risky.**
CH-01 is only drawing 52.6 kW. Even if you stopped it, the saving is modest, while the risk of losing chilled water to critical loads (server room, process cooling) is not worth it at this low plant load.

**Better options if you want to save:**
- Raise the chilled-water setpoint by +1 °C, which the heat-wave SOP allows and reduces chiller load ~4% [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 6: during the peak].
- The bigger, safer wins are the air system: AC-01 (air compressor) is running flat-out at 100% [data: get_equipment_status], and there's a known compressed-air leak scenario (S4) — fixing compressor run-time and leaks typically saves far more than shedding a partially-loaded chiller.

Bottom line: CH-01 is the active lead chiller running at low load while the plant sits at 40% of contract, so switching it off now would remove essential cooling capacity for little energy benefit. I'd hold off.

I have the complete answer from the documents.

According to **SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown**, a reflow oven in standby draws **36% of its 70 kW rating = 25.2 kW** for as long as it is left running, whereas a properly switched-off oven uses only about 340–350 kWh per oven-weekend. That's why ovens must be switched fully off rather than left in standby — standby is a continuous ~25.2 kW drain producing nothing, which is the single largest source of weekend idle energy.

For **incident S5 (2025-10-17 to 2025-10-20)**, RF-02 was left in standby all weekend: weekend energy was about **1,556 kWh** versus about **346 kWh** normal, an excess of about **1,210 kWh** from a single oven.

Note: the off-schedule rule only flags this after 120 minutes above 20% of rating, so the real benefit comes from switching the ovens off proactively — after the 30-minute warm-up period and only when no boards are inside.

## Load Shed Order (SOP-03)

**Shed first:** EV charging (EV-01) — paused at 100%, because it has no effect on production. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order]

The full playbook order is:

| Order | Action | Equipment | Share of present load |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Pause EV charging** | EV-01 | 100% |
| 2 | Delay the next burn-in loading | BI-01, BI-02 | 35% |
| 3 | Raise chilled-water setpoint +1 °C | CH-01, CH-02 | 4% |
| 4 | Lower compressed-air pressure 0.5 bar | AC-01, AC-02, AC-03 | 3.5% |

[source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order]

**Loads that must never be shed:**
- The server room
- Running molders mid-cycle
- Reflow ovens with boards inside

[source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order]

The order deliberately puts the least disruptive actions first, with EV charging paused first since it doesn't affect production. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Load-shed playbook]
